To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sensitivity of grass species (including monocotyledonous weeds) to important classes of herbicides inhibiting the enzyme ACCase (acety-CoA carboxlyase) is associated specifically with a particular inhibition of the multifuctional ACCase located within the plastids of these plants.
the sensitivity of grass species (e.g. maize) to important classes of herbicides inhibiting acetyl-CoA-carboxylase (ACCase) correlates with herbicide binding co-operativeity on this enzyme.
the insensitivity of grasses to important classes of herbicides is associated with herbicide-binding cooperativity, which is a property that is not present in sensitive forms of the same enzyme.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biochemical characterization of the ACCase isoforms from a range of plant species.
the biochemical characterization of the ACCase isoforms from grass species that are insensitive to graminicides, and the identification of the molecular determinants that confer insensitivity.
the biochemical characterization of ACCase isoforms in grasses and dicotyledons and with the elucidation of the biochemical basis of the resistance to ACCase-inhibitor herbicides.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
herbicide-binding co-operation is an important property that correlates with graminicide insensitivity of ACCase in grasses.
graminicide sensitivity of grasses is associated with herbicide-binding non-co-operativity, whereas insensitivity is correlated with binding co-operativity.
the graminicides inhibit the grass ACCase in a co-operative fashion, and that this is the only kinetic difference that can be found between the sensitive and the insensitive forms of ACCase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
herbicide binding to ACCase in grasses is a co-operative process, and that this co-operativity is a major feature of insensitive forms of the enzyme.

the insensitivity of grasses to graminicide herbicide inhibition of ACCase is associated with herbicide-binding cooperativity, and that this property is not related to the ability to carboxylase propionyl-Coa.

the insensitivity of the ACCases from resistant grasses is due to a change in the conformation of the enzyme that results in the binding of graminicides to the enzyme being co-operative rather than non-co-operative, and that this change in conformation is due to the presence of a specific mutation in the enzyme.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sensitivity of ACCase to graminicides is associated with herbicide binding co-operative properties, and not with any other biochemical or kinetic properties of the enzyme.
the insensitivity of grasses to graminicides is associated with the presence of herbicide-binding co-operative ACCase isoforms.
herbicide-binding co-operation is the only kinetic feature that differentiates insensitive from sensitive ACCases.
